Economic Democracy Now: A Case for Worker Ownership

Fellow citizens, workers, and believers in democracy—

We gather today at a crossroads. For over two centuries, we have fought and bled and marched for the principle that those affected by decisions should have a voice in making them. We call this democracy, and we hold it sacred.

Yet every morning, millions of us walk through doors into spaces where democracy does not follow. We clock in, and our rights as citizens dissolve. We become subjects—not participants—in the institutions that consume the majority of our waking lives.

This is the great unfinished business of the democratic project.

The Contradiction We Live

We would never accept a political system where one person—or a small board of distant shareholders—could dictate the laws of our communities, determine our schedules, surveil our movements, and dismiss us at will with no recourse, no voice, no vote.

And yet we accept this as normal in our workplaces.

We call ourselves free, but the average worker has more say in who wins a reality television show than in the fundamental conditions of their daily labor.

Think about that.

You can vote for president. You can vote for your city council. But the institution that determines whether you can pay rent, whether you can see a doctor, whether you can provide for your children—you have no vote there at all.

This is not freedom. This is the residue of an older world—a world of lords and serfs dressed up in modern clothing.

The Promise of Worker Ownership

But there is another way. There has always been another way.

Across this nation and around the world, worker-owned cooperatives prove every single day that democracy in the workplace is not a utopian dream—it is a practical, achievable, thriving reality.

Mondragon in Spain—over 80,000 worker-owners, one of the largest corporations in the country, weathering recessions that devastate traditional firms, because when times get hard, workers vote to reduce hours rather than eliminate their neighbors.

The Emilia-Romagna region of Italy—where cooperatives drive one of the most productive, innovative economies in Europe.

Right here at home—credit unions, food co-ops, employee-owned firms that consistently show higher productivity, lower turnover, greater resilience, and yes—greater equality.

These are not experiments. These are successes. And they point toward a fundamental truth:

People work harder, smarter, and with greater dignity when they have a stake. When they have a voice. When they are owners, not renters, of their economic lives.

Why Mandates Matter

Now, some will say: "If cooperatives are so great, let the market decide. Let them emerge naturally."

But we know better.

We know that slave-owners did not voluntarily free their slaves because someone demonstrated the economic efficiency of free labor.

We know that factory owners did not voluntarily end child labor because a cooperative showed it wasn't necessary.

We know that those who hold power rarely surrender it out of rational persuasion alone.

The business structures we inherit are not the product of natural law. They are the product of historical choices—legal frameworks written to favor concentrated ownership, capital over labor, shareholders over stakeholders.

We did not get the forty-hour week through polite suggestion. We did not get workplace safety through market forces. We won these through collective action and through law.

And so it must be with economic democracy.

We must write into law what justice demands: that workers have the right not merely to sell their labor, but to own it. That those who create wealth with their hands, their minds, and their time should govern how that wealth is created and distributed.

The Moral Case

Let me speak plainly about justice.

When a worker gives forty years to a company and is discarded without a pension—that is injustice.

When executives who produce nothing take home hundreds of times what workers who produce everything take home—that is injustice.

When a handful of shareholders who have never set foot in a factory can vote to close it and devastate a community—that is injustice.

When we tell workers they must be "grateful for the opportunity" to enrich someone else—that is the language of servitude, not freedom.

The worker cooperative is the structural answer to structural injustice.

Not charity. Not benevolent bosses. Not trickle-down promises that never trickle.

Ownership. Real power. A seat at the table that cannot be taken away.

Answering the Critics

To those who say this is radical, I say: What is radical is accepting that the economy should operate on principles we reject everywhere else.

To those who say this will harm efficiency, I point to the evidence—decades of research showing cooperatives match or exceed traditional firms in productivity while distributing rewards far more fairly.

To those who say we cannot force businesses to change, I remind you: We already tell businesses what they can and cannot do. We set minimum wages. We prohibit discrimination. We require safety standards. We charter corporations through public law. There is no business that exists outside the social contract.

We are simply asking to renegotiate that contract—to write in what should have been there from the beginning.

To those who say this is socialism, I say: This is democracy. This is workers owning the fruits of their labor. If anything, this is the most authentic capitalism imaginable—capital in the hands of those who create value, not extracted by those who merely hold paper.

The World We Could Build

Imagine an economy where the people who grow our food have a voice in how it's grown.

Where the nurses who heal us help decide how hospitals are run.

Where teachers shape educational policy, not distant administrators.

Where factory workers can vote against moving jobs overseas to pad shareholder returns.

Where layoffs are the last resort, not the first quarterly adjustment.

Where the gap between the highest and lowest paid is determined by the workers themselves—and is, everywhere cooperatives exist, a fraction of what we see in traditional corporations.

Where the profits of enterprise flow back into communities, into wages, into investment—not into stock buybacks and offshore accounts.

This is not a fantasy. This is a choice.

Every element of that vision exists, right now, somewhere in the world. We simply lack the collective will to make it universal.

A Call to Action

So I call on legislators: Draft the bills. Mandate transition timelines for medium and large businesses. Create the financing mechanisms, the technical assistance programs, the legal frameworks that make conversion practical.

I call on workers: Organize. Demand not just better wages, but ownership. Your labor built these companies. Your labor should govern them.

I call on citizens: Support cooperative businesses today. Bank at credit unions. Shop at co-ops. Show with your choices what you want to see in law.

And I call on all of us to reject the poverty of imagination that says the economy must be what it has always been.

We ended monarchy. We ended slavery. We ended child labor. We won the vote for those excluded. At every stage, those who benefited from the old order said change was impossible, impractical, against human nature.

They were wrong then. They are wrong now.

Conclusion

My friends, democracy is not a gift given to us by the powerful. It is a practice we must extend into every corner of our lives.

For too long, we have accepted a world where we are citizens in the morning and subjects by nine o'clock.

For too long, we have accepted that democracy stops at the factory gates, the office doors, the warehouse entrances.

It is time—past time—to finish what democracy started.

Let us build an economy worthy of free people.

Let us build an economy where your voice matters not just in the voting booth, but in the place where you spend most of your waking life.

Let us build an economy owned by the many, governed by the many, and for the benefit of the many.

Let us build economic democracy—and let us begin today.

Thank you.

The Democratic Workplace: A Case for Mandatory Worker Ownership

Introduction

The organization of economic life is among the most consequential political choices a society makes, yet modern democracies have largely treated the internal governance of corporations as beyond democratic scrutiny. We accept, almost without examination, an arrangement in which the majority of working adults spend the majority of their waking hours in institutions that are effectively autocratic — where decisions about their livelihoods, working conditions, and economic futures are made by owners and executives to whom they owe obedience but from whom they receive no reciprocal accountability. This essay argues that this arrangement is both ethically indefensible and economically suboptimal, and that mandatory conversion of medium-to-large businesses into democratically controlled worker-owned cooperatives represents a necessary and proportionate policy response.

The Ethical Foundation: Democracy Cannot Stop at the Factory Gate

The foundational principle of liberal democratic theory is that legitimate authority requires the consent of the governed. We justify democratic political institutions on exactly this basis — that those subject to power should have meaningful voice in how it is exercised. Yet this principle, applied consistently, demands far more than periodic elections for legislators. It demands examination of every institution that exercises substantial power over human lives.

The modern corporation exercises extraordinary power. It determines whether workers can afford housing, healthcare, and education for their children. It shapes the pace, content, and conditions of their daily existence. It can unilaterally eliminate their economic security through layoffs, relocation, or restructuring. In many company towns and specialized industries, the power of a single employer approaches the totality of what political theorist Robert Dahl called "governance" — the binding direction of behavior through institutionalized authority.

Philosopher Elizabeth Anderson has argued compellingly that the private employment relationship constitutes a form of private government, one that operates largely outside constitutional protections that citizens rightly demand from the state. Workers may be told how to dress, speak, move, and think during working hours. They may be disciplined for conduct outside the workplace. They may be surveilled with an intimacy no democratic state could legally exercise over citizens. All of this is justified by the fiction of voluntary contract — you agreed to the terms, therefore they are legitimate.

This fiction deserves direct challenge. Consent obtained under conditions of economic compulsion is not meaningfully free. When the alternative to accepting an employer's authority is poverty, homelessness, or inability to provide for dependents, the "voluntary" nature of the employment contract is substantially compromised. As political philosopher Samuel Bowles has noted, the wage relationship is characterized by a fundamental power asymmetry — the employer's need for any particular worker is almost always less urgent than the worker's need for employment. This asymmetry vitiates the consent that supposedly legitimizes managerial authority.

The ethical case for worker ownership and democratic control is therefore rooted in the most basic commitments of liberal political philosophy: that human dignity requires self-governance, that legitimate authority requires consent, and that consent requires genuine alternatives. Mandatory conversion to worker cooperatives does not impose an alien value system on democratic societies — it extends the democratic values those societies already profess to their most pervasive and consequential institutions.

Furthermore, there is the matter of distributive justice. Contemporary economies have generated extraordinary wealth through the collaborative efforts of workers, communities, and accumulated social knowledge. The returns from this collaboration have been captured to a striking degree by capital owners rather than labor. In the United States, the share of national income going to labor has declined substantially since the 1970s, while corporate profits and returns to capital have reached historic highs. Worker ownership directly addresses this imbalance not through redistribution after the fact but through restructuring the underlying ownership relationships that determine distribution in the first place. This is not charity or redistribution — it is justice in the original sense, rendering to each participant in productive enterprise their appropriate share of what they have helped create.

The Economic Case: Cooperation as Productive Principle

Critics of mandatory worker ownership typically argue from economic efficiency — that market competition, private ownership, and hierarchical management optimize productivity and innovation in ways that democratic governance cannot match. This argument rests on empirical claims that are far weaker than their confident assertion suggests, and there are strong theoretical and empirical grounds for expecting worker-owned cooperatives to perform as well or better than conventional firms across most economically significant dimensions.

Productivity and Alignment of Incentives

Standard economic theory actually predicts that worker ownership should improve productive efficiency, because it resolves one of the fundamental problems of conventional employment: the principal-agent problem. In a conventional firm, workers are agents hired to serve principals (shareholders and managers) whose interests diverge from their own. Workers have inherent incentives to supply less effort than employers would prefer, requiring costly monitoring, supervision, and incentive structures. This is not a moral failing of workers — it is a rational response to an incentive structure in which the rewards of effort flow primarily to owners rather than to those who provide it.

Worker ownership transforms this dynamic. When workers are owners, the effort-reward relationship is fundamentally altered. Work harder and more effectively, and you directly share in the resulting prosperity. This alignment of incentives should, by standard economic reasoning, reduce monitoring costs, improve effort provision, and increase overall productive efficiency. The empirical literature largely confirms this theoretical prediction. Studies of worker cooperatives across multiple countries and industries find that they are generally as productive as or more productive than comparable conventional firms, with several meta-analyses finding modest but consistent productivity advantages.

The Mondragon Corporation in the Basque region of Spain represents perhaps the most studied large-scale example of worker cooperative economics. Founded in 1956, Mondragon has grown into a federation of over 80 cooperatives employing more than 80,000 worker-owners, operating across manufacturing, retail, finance, and education. While Mondragon has faced real challenges and has made compromises that cooperative purists criticize, its basic performance demonstrates that large-scale complex economic activity is entirely compatible with democratic worker governance. It is not a utopian exception — it is an existence proof.

Wage Inequality and Economic Stability

Worker cooperatives consistently demonstrate dramatically compressed wage ratios between highest and lowest paid workers compared to conventional corporations. In conventional Fortune 500 companies, CEO-to-median-worker pay ratios commonly exceed 300:1 and sometimes reach into the thousands. In worker cooperatives, ratios above 10:1 are rare, and many cooperatives maintain ratios below 5:1 as a matter of democratic principle. This compression is economically significant beyond its obvious equity implications.

High wage inequality undermines aggregate demand. When income concentrates at the top, a larger share goes to saving and investment rather than consumption, reducing the spending that sustains employment across the economy. More broadly, extreme inequality has been associated empirically with lower social mobility, worse health outcomes, higher rates of crime and social dysfunction, and reduced political equality — as concentrated wealth translates into concentrated political influence. Mandatory worker ownership would address wage inequality at its structural source rather than through the blunt and often-contested instruments of progressive taxation and redistribution.

Worker cooperatives also demonstrate greater employment stability during economic downturns. Research on cooperatives in multiple countries shows that they are substantially less likely to respond to demand shocks through layoffs than conventional firms of comparable size and sector. When revenue falls, cooperative members face a genuine collective choice: reduce hours or wages across the board, or cut some members' employment entirely. Democratic deliberation among people who know and work with each other, and who share ownership stakes, tends strongly toward the former. The result is that cooperative employment functions as an automatic stabilizer — dampening rather than amplifying economic cycles.

This has macroeconomic significance beyond individual firms. However, this argument has less force for the medium-to-large established firms that would be the primary targets of mandatory conversion policy. Large established corporations face their own characteristic failure modes: short-termism driven by quarterly earnings pressure, excessive focus on financial engineering rather than productive investment, and the prioritization of shareholder returns through buybacks and dividends over R&D and worker development. Worker owners, whose wealth is bound up in the long-term health of their firm, have stronger incentives for genuine productive investment than shareholders who can easily diversify and exit.

Moreover, the organizational literature on innovation consistently finds that it emerges not from top-down direction by managers but from the creative engagement of workers closest to productive processes. Toyota's famous production system, which spawned lean manufacturing practices now adopted globally, was built on the principle that production workers possess knowledge and insight that engineers and managers cannot replicate from above, and that continuous improvement requires engaging that knowledge systematically. Democratic workplace governance is structurally better suited to harnessing worker knowledge and creativity than hierarchical management that treats workers as replaceable inputs.

The Transition Costs Objection

The most practically serious objection to mandatory conversion concerns transition costs and disruption. Converting large numbers of businesses to new ownership structures in compressed timeframes could damage productivity, create legal uncertainty, and generate resistance that undermines both economic performance and political stability.

This objection argues for careful implementation, not against the policy itself. A well-designed mandatory conversion framework should phase implementation over a decade or more, beginning with the largest corporations and proceeding to medium-sized businesses as institutional infrastructure develops. It should provide clear legal frameworks for conversion, financial support mechanisms to enable worker buyouts at fair valuations, and technical assistance for workers learning to exercise democratic governance. The policy should treat existing shareholders fairly — not through expropriation but through buyouts at fair market value, financed through long-term worker-owned debt and equity arrangements of the kind that have successfully enabled cooperative conversions in Italy, Spain, and elsewhere.

Italy's Marcora Law provides a useful model. Since 1985, it has enabled worker buyouts of failing businesses, allowing workers to use their severance entitlements as capital and providing matching funds from a national cooperative development fund. Thousands of businesses have been converted under this framework, preserving employment and creating stable worker-owned enterprises. A mandatory framework would be more ambitious but could draw on similar financing mechanisms.

A related objection concerns capital allocation: without equity markets pricing firms and directing capital toward its most productive uses, how would a cooperative economy allocate investment efficiently? This is a genuine concern but again a manageable one. Worker cooperatives can and do access debt financing from banks, cooperative development funds, and ethical investment vehicles. They can issue non-voting equity to external investors while retaining democratic control. The Mondragon cooperatives operate their own cooperative bank. There is no inherent reason why democratic worker governance prevents access to capital — it requires adapted financial institutions rather than the abandonment of capital markets altogether.

Some argue that democratic governance would prevent worker-owned cooperatives from attracting and retaining the managerial talent necessary for complex large-scale organizations. This objection underestimates the degree to which managerial compensation in conventional corporations reflects bargaining power rather than scarce talent, and overestimates the difficulty of attracting skilled managers to well-compensated positions in democratic organizations. The habits of collective deliberation, compromise, and shared decision-making cultivated in democratic workplaces are precisely the capacities that self-governance requires.

The case for mandatory conversion of medium-to-large businesses to democratically controlled worker cooperatives rests on foundations that are both principled and practical. Ethically, the authority that corporations exercise over workers' lives cannot be legitimated through contracts that are only formally voluntary, and the distribution of economic returns from collective productive effort demands justice rather than the perpetuation of ownership structures inherited from a less democratic era. Economically, worker ownership aligns incentives, reduces inequality, stabilizes employment, and engages the creativity and knowledge of all participants in production rather than reserving decision-making for a small managerial elite.

The objections to this policy — concerning transition costs, capital allocation, and managerial expertise — are serious and deserve serious answers, but they are answers available within a carefully designed implementation framework rather than fundamental obstacles. The international evidence from Mondragon, Italian cooperative districts, and democratic workplaces across diverse sectors demonstrates that large-scale complex economic activity is entirely compatible with democratic worker governance.

The deeper question is whether we are willing to take democracy seriously — not merely as a system for selecting governments every few years, but as a principle of legitimate authority that extends to all institutions that exercise substantial power over human lives. If we are, the democratic workplace is not a utopian fantasy. It is an institutional necessity.

Introduction

Ethical Reasons

  • Worker Empowerment and Dignity: Mandatory WOCs would empower employees by granting them decision-making power and ensuring their voices are heard. This democratization of the workplace upholds human dignity by acknowledging workers' rights to control the fruits of their labor (Dahl, 1985).

  • Improved Productivity and Innovation: Worker ownership and participation enhance productivity and innovativeness, as employees are more invested in their work when they share in the rewards.   • Stimulating Local Economies: WOCs preferentially source and spend locally, keeping wealth circulating within communities and stimulating local economic development. This multiplier effect can significantly bolster regional economies (Zeuli & Cropp, 2004).

To realize these ethical and economic benefits, policymakers should introduce legislation requiring medium-to-large businesses to transition into WOCs over a reasonable period. Mandatory implementation of worker-owned cooperatives for medium-to-large businesses is a powerful means to address inequities, empower workers, and promote economic resilience. Worker Cooperatives & Mandated Transition: Potential Benefits & Rationales

The idea of transitioning medium-to-large businesses into worker-owned cooperatives, where employees democratically control the firm, is gaining traction as a potential economic model. Here's a breakdown of the supposed benefits and rationales often cited for mandating such a shift, presented factually:

I. Core Concept: Worker Cooperatives

Before discussing a mandate, it’s crucial to understand the model. A worker cooperative is an enterprise owned and democratically governed by its employees. Key characteristics include:

  • One Worker, One Vote: Decision-making power is distributed equally among workers, regardless of their position or investment.
  • Shared Profits: Profits are distributed to workers based on their labor contribution, not capital investment.
  • Worker Participation: Workers participate actively in the strategic direction and operation of the business.
  • Collective Ownership: The cooperative is owned as a collective rather than by individual shareholders.

II. Arguments for Mandating Transition (and benefits proponents claim would result):

The rationale for mandating this transition (a much stronger proposal than incentizing it) generally rests on several pillars:

A. Economic Equality & Reduced Inequality:

  • Wealth Distribution: A significant argument is that it addresses growing wealth inequality. By transferring ownership to workers, more economic benefits flow to a broader base of the population rather than accumulating in the hands of shareholders. This is particularly relevant as the gap between executive compensation and worker wages widens.
  • Fairer Income: Cooperatives tend to have lower CEO-to-worker pay ratios than conventional corporations. Studies suggest worker co-ops distribute a larger proportion of revenue to labor. (Fonte: Democracy at Work Institute)
  • Resilience to Economic Shocks: Proponents argue employee-ownership creates greater financial stability for workers during economic downturns as they are directly invested in the survival of the business.

B. Improved Workplace Dynamics & Productivity:

  • Increased Motivation & Engagement: Worker ownership aims to increase employee motivation and engagement by giving them a direct stake in the company's success. This often leads to higher job satisfaction. Research suggests cooperative workplaces experience greater employee commitment. (Fonte: Journal of Cooperative Studies)
  • Enhanced Productivity: Increased engagement and a sense of ownership can translate into higher productivity, as workers are more likely to contribute their best efforts. Some studies (though debated) indicate worker co-ops are as productive, or even more productive, than conventional firms. (Fonte: Employee Ownership and Productivity, Kruse)
  • Reduced Turnover: Greater job satisfaction and security lead to lower employee turnover rates, reducing recruitment and training costs.
  • Improved Workplace Democracy: The democratic structure fosters a more participatory and empowering work environment, potentially leading to better working conditions.

C. Long-Term Economic Stability & Societal Benefits:

  • Local Economic Development: Cooperatives are often more rooted in local communities, reinvesting profits locally and supporting local economies.
  • Long-Term Investment Strategy: Because worker-owners are invested in the long-term success of the business (and live with the consequences of short-sighted decisions), they are theoretically less likely to prioritize maximizing short-term profits at the expense of long-term sustainability.
  • Increased Innovation: A more democratic environment can encourage more diverse perspectives and open communication leading to increased innovation.
  • Reduced Risk of Financial Crisis: Some proponents suggest widespread worker ownership could mitigate systemic financial risk by reducing the power of speculative capital and incentivizing responsible business practices.

III. Proposed Methods of Mandated Transition (and associated complexities):

The method of transition would be a major point of debate. Commonly discussed approaches include:

  • Gradual Transition: Businesses could be given a timeframe (e.g., 5-10 years) to transition a certain percentage of ownership to employees each year.
  • Tax Incentives & Credit Access Favored for Cooperative Conversions: Instead of a pure mandate, a system could incentivize conversions.
  • Sector-Specific Transitions: Mandates might initially apply to specific sectors deemed particularly prone to exploitation or instability.
  • Employee Stock Ownership Plans (ESOPs) as an Interim Step: ESOPs, while not fully democratic, could be used as a stepping stone toward full worker cooperative ownership.

IV. Potential Challenges & Criticisms of a Mandate:

A mandated transition would face substantial challenges and criticisms:

  • Capital Flight/Business Relocation: Concerns exist that businesses might relocate to avoid worker ownership requirements.
  • Management Expertise/Skill Gap: Successfully running a business requires specific skills. Concerns that workers may lack the necessary expertise in finance, marketing or strategy. Training and professional development would be crucial, and costly.
  • Decision-Making Complexity: Democratic decision-making can be slower and more complex than hierarchical structures.
  • Valuation and Ownership Transfer: Determining the fair value of a business and transferring ownership can be legally and financially complex.
  • Resistance from Existing Owners: Business owners are likely to resist relinquishing control, leading to legal challenges and political opposition.
  • Practical Implementation: Creating a workable legal framework for large-scale worker cooperative ownership would require significant legislative effort.
  • Potential for "Tragedy of the Commons": Without effective governance structures, worker-owners may prioritize short-term gains over long-term sustainability.

V. Conclusion:

Mandating worker cooperative transitions represents a radical shift in economic structures. Proponents argue it offers the potential for a more equitable, stable, and democratic economy. However, it faces significant practical challenges and legitimate concerns about implementation and potential unintended consequences. A thorough consideration of the benefits, drawbacks, and practical complexities is crucial before implementing such a sweeping policy change.

Model Response:

The Case for Democratic Enterprise: Why Worker-Owned Cooperatives Should Be Mandatory for Medium-to-Large Firms

I. The Democratic Deficit in Economic Life

We accept, almost without thinking, that democratic governance is the only legitimate form of political authority in a free society. We would not tolerate a monarchy or a dictatorship in Washington or Brussels or Beijing — not because monarchs and dictators are necessarily incompetent, but because the concentration of unchecked power in the hands of the few is, in itself, a violation of the dignity and agency of the many.

And yet, in the economic sphere — where we spend a third of our waking lives, where the decisions made shape the texture of our days, the security of our families, and the futures of our communities — we tolerate something remarkably close to authoritarianism. The typical medium-to-large enterprise is governed by a board of directors elected by shareholders, who are themselves unelected. Workers, who collectively generate the firm's value, have little or no formal voice in the decisions that determine their wages, their working conditions, their job security, and the broader direction of the enterprise.

This essay argues that this is not merely an aesthetic or philosophical failing — it is a deep structural injustice that produces measurable economic harm, and that it can, and should, be remedied through law. Specifically, I argue that all medium-to-large businesses should be required to convert into democratically controlled worker-owned cooperatives.

II. The Ethical Foundation

A. The Principle of Self-Governance

The philosophical case for worker cooperatives rests on a principle that most political traditions share, despite their other disagreements: that people who are affected by a decision have a right to participate in making it. This principle, articulated in different forms by Aristotle, the Enlightenment social contract theorists, and the traditions of labor solidarity, holds that political legitimacy arises not from the consent of a distant electorate but from the ongoing, material involvement of those whose lives are at stake.

In a conventional firm, workers are subject to decisions they had no hand in shaping. They can be laid off, reorganized, relocated, or have their benefits cut by executives who face no comparable vulnerability. This is not a market outcome — it is a governance outcome. And governance, when it lacks the consent of the governed, lacks legitimacy.

Worker cooperatives restore that legitimacy. When workers elect their managers, vote on strategic direction, and share in the residual profits of the firm, the relationship between the individual and the enterprise is no longer one of subordination but of participation. This is not a utopian aspiration; it is simply the application of democratic norms to a domain where they are conspicuously absent.

B. Distributive Justice

The concentration of economic power within firms produces a concentration of wealth that most societies say they oppose but structurally enforce. Consider: in a typical corporation, the ratio of CEO compensation to median worker pay exceeds 300-to-1 in many developed economies. This disparity cannot be explained solely by differences in talent or contribution. It is, in large part, a function of power — the power to set one's own compensation when one sits on the board that approves it, when one appoints the compensation committee, when the shareholders are dispersed and disengaged.

In a worker cooperative, profits are distributed among the workers themselves. This does not guarantee perfect equality, but it shifts the distribution curve dramatically. Research on the Mondragon Corporation in Spain's Basque Country — the world's largest and most successful cooperative network — shows that the ratio of highest-to-lowest pay rarely exceeds 6-to-1, compared to hundreds-to-one in conventional firms. The cooperative model does not eliminate inequality, but it constrains it through democratic accountability.

When we talk about the distribution of wealth in society, we tend to focus on tax policy and transfers. These are important. But the distribution of wealth before taxes — the market distribution — is determined largely by the internal governance of firms. If we want a more just distribution of wealth, we cannot ignore the governance structures that produce the initial distribution.

C. Dignity and Meaning at Work

The psychological literature is unambiguous: autonomy, a sense of control over one's environment, and meaningful participation in collective decisions are among the strongest predictors of well-being, mental health, and job satisfaction. The conventional firm, by concentrating decision-making authority in the hands of a few, systematically deprives most workers of these conditions.

This is not merely an inconvenience. Work occupies a central place in human life. To structure the majority of adult experience around institutions in which most people have no voice is to inflict a quiet but pervasive harm — one that manifests in alienation, disengagement, and the sense of meaninglessness that characterizes much of modern working life.

Worker cooperatives address this directly. When workers participate in governance, the psychological relationship to work changes. This is not speculative. Surveys of cooperative workers consistently show higher levels of job satisfaction, lower rates of burnout, and stronger identification with their enterprise. The cooperative model treats workers not as inputs to be managed but as participants to be engaged.

III. The Economic Case

A. Resilience and Long-Term Stability

Conventional wisdom holds that the profit motive, channeled through shareholder-owned firms, produces the most efficient allocation of resources. But this rests on assumptions that do not hold well in practice. The shareholder-owned firm is, by design, oriented toward short-term returns. Quarterly earnings reports, activist investors, and the threat of hostile takeovers create powerful incentives to prioritize immediate profitability over long-term health. The result is a systematic bias toward cutting costs — including labor costs, research and development, and maintenance — in ways that may benefit shareholders in the short term but erode the firm's productive capacity over time.

Worker cooperatives, by contrast, are not subject to the same short-term pressures. Because the workers themselves are the owners, their interests are aligned with the long-term health of the enterprise. They have no incentive to liquidate their own jobs for a quarterly earnings boost. They have every incentive to invest in the skills, infrastructure, and relationships that sustain the firm over decades.

The empirical record supports this. Research has shown that worker cooperatives have lower rates of bankruptcy, higher survival rates, and greater resilience during economic downturns. During the 2008 financial crisis, Mondragon experienced no firm closures and only modest layoffs — a record that stood in stark contrast to the mass layoffs and bankruptcies that swept through shareholder-owned firms. This resilience is not accidental; it is structural.

B. Productivity and Innovation

A common objection to worker cooperatives is that they are less productive — that the absence of the profit motive, or the inefficiency of democratic decision-making, undermines performance. The evidence does not support this.

A study by Blasi, Freeman, and Kruse published by the National Bureau of Economic Research found that firms with significant employee ownership and participation — characteristics of the cooperative model — exhibited higher productivity and lower turnover than comparable conventional firms. The mechanisms are intuitive: when workers have a stake in the enterprise, they have stronger incentives to contribute effort, to innovate, and to stay. Turnover, which is enormously costly, is reduced. Institutional knowledge is retained. Morale is higher.

As for democratic decision-making: it is true that consensus takes time. But the cooperative model does not require unanimity on every decision. Most cooperatives delegate operational decisions to elected managers and reserve democratic voting for strategic matters — much as parliamentary democracies delegate day-to-day governance to an elected executive while reserving broad policy decisions for the legislature. The result is not inefficiency but a different kind of efficiency: one that incorporates the distributed knowledge of the workforce rather than relying on the limited perspective of a small executive class.

C. Stability of the Social Fabric

The destruction of stable, well-paying jobs — particularly in manufacturing and middle-skill sectors — has been one of the defining features of the global economy in recent decades. This destruction is not inevitable; it is a consequence of the governance structures of shareholder-owned firms, which incentivize offshoring, automation, and cost-cutting that externalize the social costs onto communities.

Worker cooperatives, rooted in place and accountable to their members, have far less incentive to relocate or automate in ways that destroy local employment. They are embedded in their communities in ways that extractive firms are not. Mandatory conversion would therefore serve not only as an industrial policy but as a community policy, stabilizing the social infrastructure that shareholder-owned firms have steadily eroded.

IV. Addressing Objections

"This infringes on property rights."

Property rights are not natural facts; they are legal constructions, defined and enforced by the state. We already constrain property rights extensively — through zoning laws, environmental regulations, labor laws, antitrust statutes, and a host of other mechanisms. The question is never whether to constrain property rights, but how and to what end.

A mandatory conversion law would not seize property without compensation. It can be structured — as it has been in existing cooperative development programs — as a transition in which existing owners are compensated, workers assume ownership over time through dedicated savings funds or state-backed financing, and the transition is phased and orderly. The principle is not expropriation but reorientation: just as we require firms to comply with safety regulations regardless of their owners' preferences, we can require them to comply with democratic governance standards regardless of their owners' preferences.

"Workers don't want to be owners."

This objection is empirically weak and philosophically inconsistent. Surveys consistently show that a majority of workers express interest in ownership and governance roles when the option is available. The Mondragon system, with over 80,000 worker-owners, is itself a refutation of this claim.

Moreover, the fact that some workers may prefer to avoid governance responsibilities does not invalidate the policy, any more than the fact that some citizens may not vote invalidates democracy. The right to participate is not a burden; it is a protection. Those who do not wish to exercise it actively can choose minimal participation, but the institutional structure ensures that the concentration of power in the hands of a few is prevented.

"Cooperatives can't scale."

This claim was once more tenable, but the evidence has moved decisively. Mondragon operates in banking, retail, manufacturing, and education, with over €12 billion in annual revenue. Cooperative networks such as Coop57 in Italy and the Cooperative Group in the United Kingdom demonstrate that the model can function at significant scale across multiple sectors. The Mondragon cooperative university, Mondragon University, is itself one of the top-rated universities in Spain, demonstrating that the model extends well beyond manufacturing.

"What would this look like?" you ask.

It would look like workers electing their own leadership—not from a boardroom chosen by anonymous shareholders, but from among themselves, by people who understand the work because they do the work.

It would look like profits being distributed not to distant capital, but to the communities where value is actually created—reinvested in wages, in benefits, in local schools and infrastructure.

It would look like a company like Amazon—or Boeing, or Walmart, or Tesla—run not as the fiefdom of a single visionary (or a single tyrant, depending on your perspective), but as a commonwealth, governed by the principle that those who contribute the labor deserve a seat at the table where the decisions are made.

And here is what I need you to understand: this is not a fantasy. This is already happening.

[PART III — The Evidence]

Mondragon. A city in the Basque Country of Spain, where a network of over 95 worker cooperatives employs more than 80,000 people. During the 2008 financial crisis—when corporate layoffs swept through Europe like a plague—Mondragon did not fire a single worker. Instead, they reduced hours, rotated positions, and shared the burden. Because when the workers are the owners, you don't solve a crisis by destroying livelihoods. You solve it together.

In the United States, the Evergreen Cooperatives of Cleveland, Ohio have lifted hundreds of families out of poverty by creating worker-owned laundry, solar, and urban farming enterprises in neighborhoods that Fortune 500 companies had abandoned decades ago.

The Emilia-Romagna region of Italy—home to one of the most productive economies in Europe—is powered in large part by cooperatives. Not as a quaint alternative. As the backbone of the regional economy.

This is not ideology. This is data.

But let me move beyond economics for a moment, because this is not merely a question of efficiency. This is a question of justice.

When a worker spends twenty years building a company—showing up every day, solving problems, training new hires, maintaining the machinery that makes the enterprise possible—and that worker has no claim to the value they created, no voice in the decisions that affect their life, no ownership stake in the institution they sustain—what do we call that?

We call it legal. We call it the market. We call it the way things are.

But I call it what it is: a moral failure.

The argument for worker cooperatives is, at its heart, the same argument that Thomas Jefferson made for democratic government. He wrote, and I quote: "Whenever a man has cast a longing eye on offices, a rottenness begins in his conduct." The concentration of power—whether political or economic—corrupts. It distorts. It dehumanizes.

The cooperative model is not utopian. It is republican in the deepest sense of the word: it insists that power must be distributed, that authority must derive from consent, and that the governed must have a voice in their governance.

"This will destroy entrepreneurship."

"Workers don't want the responsibility."

This is not socialism. This is democracy extended to its logical conclusion.

And so I stand before you today and make this argument:

That the economy belongs to the people who power it. That wealth created by collective labor should be governed by collective consent. That the workplace—the place where we spend the majority of our waking lives—should be a site of freedom, not a site of submission.

  • And phases out the concentrated ownership models that have allowed a shrinking class of owners to exercise disproportionate control over the economic lives of millions.

This is not a radical proposal. This is the completion of a radical promise—a promise made at the founding of this nation, that the people shall govern, that power shall derive from consent, and that no one shall rule over others without their say.

I will close with this.

There is a painting in the halls of our capitol that depicts the signing of the Declaration of Independence. And in that painting, you will find not kings, not aristocrats, not CEOs—but workers. They fought for self-governance.

Let us prove it.
